name: Quality Attribute Scenario
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Six Parts, No Ambiguity: Writing a Quality Attribute Scenario
lesson.summary: A quality attribute scenario turns a raw idea from scenario generation into a precise, six part statement that architects can actually evaluate against a design.
lesson.body:
A quality attribute scenario is the formal unit ATAM analyzes. It has six parts: a stimulus, the event that triggers the scenario; a source of stimulus, who or what causes it; an environment, the condition the system is in when the stimulus arrives; an artifact, the part of the system being stimulated; a response, what the system should do; and a response measure, a way to check whether the response actually happened well enough. Writing all six parts is what separates an engineering requirement from a slogan. Secure blockchain is not a quality attribute scenario. The six part version is.

Take a raw idea from scenario generation, a fear that a large miner could rewrite recent history, and turn it into a full scenario. Source of stimulus: an attacker who has assembled more than fifty percent of the network's hashing power. Stimulus: the attacker attempts to replace the six most recently confirmed blocks with an alternative chain that reverses a payment. Environment: normal network operation, no prior partition. Artifact: the proof of work consensus mechanism and the exchanges relying on its finality guarantees. Response: the alternative chain either fails to outpace the honest chain, or the attack's cost in wasted computation exceeds the value the attacker could steal. Response measure: exchanges that wait for six confirmations are not defrauded, and the cost of a successful attack is quantifiably higher than the funds it could capture.

This structure matters because every one of the six parts is a separate axis a system could fail on. A blockchain might handle the stimulus correctly under one environment, say normal load, but fail under another, say a period of unusually low overall network hash rate that makes a fifty one percent attack temporarily cheaper. Writing the environment explicitly is what catches that gap; a vague requirement like resistant to fifty one percent attacks would not.

Quality attribute scenarios are not limited to security. A performance scenario for a smart contract platform might read: source, a popular NFT mint event; stimulus, ten thousand wallets submit transactions within the same sixty second window; environment, peak load, mempool already near capacity; artifact, the transaction ordering and fee market mechanism; response, transactions are still included within a bounded number of blocks and fees rise predictably rather than becoming unusable; response measure, ninety five percent of submitted transactions confirm within twenty minutes at a fee the sending wallet had budgeted for. This is exactly the kind of scenario that, when written honestly, exposes gas price spikes as a real architectural weakness rather than an unfortunate but unavoidable fact of blockchain life.

Once a set of quality attribute scenarios exists, they become the raw material for the next ATAM artifact, the utility tree, which organizes and prioritizes them so a review team knows which handful, out of the dozens generated, deserve the limited time available for architectural analysis.
